notes:
Carbohydrates

  • Classified as monosaccharides (glucose, fructose — cannot be hydrolysed further), oligosaccharides (2–10 units, e.g. disaccharides sucrose/maltose/lactose), and polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen).
  • Reducing sugars (free –CHO or –OH forming one, reduce Fehling's/Tollens'): glucose, fructose, maltose, lactose. Non-reducing: sucrose (glycosidic bond involves both anomeric carbons).
  • Glucose: open chain gives 2,4-DNP test, forms oxime with NH$_2$OH, gets acetylated (5 –OH groups confirmed by pentaacetate) — but cyclic (pyranose, hemiacetal) form is the more stable, predominant structure explaining absence of some aldehyde reactions and existence of $\alpha$/$\beta$ anomers.
  • Starch: amylose (linear, $\alpha$-1,4 glycosidic links, water-soluble) + amylopectin (branched, $\alpha$-1,4 and $\alpha$-1,6). Cellulose: linear, $\beta$-1,4 glycosidic links (not digestible by humans). Glycogen: highly branched, animal storage form ('animal starch').

Proteins

  • Amino acids: NH$_2$ and COOH on same (α) carbon; exist as zwitterions (dipolar ions) — this explains high melting points and water solubility.
  • Essential (must be from diet, e.g. valine, leucine) vs non-essential (body can synthesise, e.g. glycine, alanine).
  • Peptide bond = amide bond (–CO–NH–) between COOH of one amino acid and NH$_2$ of another, with loss of water.
  • Protein structure: primary (amino acid sequence) → secondary ($\alpha$-helix/$\beta$-pleated sheet, H-bonding) → tertiary (3D folding, overall shape) → quaternary (assembly of subunits, e.g. haemoglobin).
  • Denaturation: loss of secondary/tertiary structure (by heat, pH, heavy metals) with loss of biological activity; primary structure (sequence) unaffected.

Enzymes & vitamins

  • Enzymes are biocatalysts (globular proteins), highly specific (lock-and-key model), active only in a narrow pH/temperature range.
  • Vitamins classified as fat-soluble (A, D, E, K — stored in body) and water-soluble (B-complex, C — must be supplied regularly, excess excreted).
  • Deficiency diseases: A → night blindness (xerophthalmia); B$_1$ → beri-beri; B$_2$ → cheilosis; B$_6$ → convulsions; B$_{12}$ → pernicious anaemia; C → scurvy; D → rickets; K → increased blood clotting time.

Nucleic acids

ComponentDNARNA
Sugar2-deoxyriboseribose
Pyrimidine basecytosine, thyminecytosine, uracil
Purine basesadenine, guanine (both)adenine, guanine (both)
Strandsdouble helixusually single
  • Base pairing: A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds) in DNA. Nucleoside = sugar + base; nucleotide = sugar + base + phosphate.
  • DNA carries genetic information and replicates; RNA (m-RNA, t-RNA, r-RNA) carries out protein synthesis.

Exam tip

2–3 questions typical: reducing vs non-reducing sugars, glucose's cyclic structure evidence, protein structure levels & denaturation, vitamin deficiency diseases, and DNA vs RNA differences (sugar, bases, strands). Memorise the deficiency-disease table — it is a quick, guaranteed mark.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-reducing sugar?
questions.explanation: In sucrose, both anomeric carbons (of glucose and fructose) are involved in the glycosidic bond, leaving no free anomeric carbon to reduce Fehling's/Tollens' reagent.
questions.trick: Both anomeric carbons locked in glycosidic bond $\to$ sucrose is non-reducing.

questions.q: The cyclic (pyranose) structure of glucose best explains
options: the absence of Schiff's test and the existence of two anomeric (α and β) forms
questions.explanation: In the cyclic hemiacetal form the aldehyde carbon becomes a new stereocentre (anomeric carbon), giving α and β anomers, and glucose fails to give the Schiff's test because the free aldehyde group is masked in the ring.
questions.trick: Cyclic hemiacetal masks -CHO $\to$ no Schiff's test, but gives $\alpha$/$\beta$ anomers.

questions.q: Amino acids exist predominantly as zwitterions because
options: the –COOH group donates a proton to the –NH$_2$ group intramolecularly, forming NH$_3^+$ and COO$^-$
they have no charge at all
they are always dissolved in acid
questions.explanation: Internal proton transfer from the acidic –COOH to the basic –NH$_2$ group gives a dipolar (zwitterionic) structure, which explains the high melting points and water solubility of amino acids.
questions.trick: Internal H$^+$ transfer: -COOH to -NH$_2$ gives zwitterion (NH$_3^+$, COO$^-$).

questions.q: The secondary structure of a protein (α-helix, β-pleated sheet) is mainly stabilised by
options: hydrogen bonding between C=O and N–H groups of the peptide backbone
questions.explanation: Regular H-bonding patterns between the carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen of the polypeptide backbone hold the chain in a helix or sheet arrangement.
questions.trick: Secondary structure = H-bonds between backbone C=O and N-H, not side chains.

questions.q: Denaturation of a protein (e.g. by heating an egg) results in
options: loss of secondary and tertiary structure and biological activity, while the primary sequence remains unchanged
no change in the protein at all
breaking of the primary structure (peptide bonds) only
conversion of the protein into a carbohydrate
questions.explanation: Denaturation disrupts hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions maintaining the 3-D shape, destroying biological activity, but the covalent peptide bond sequence (primary structure) is unaffected.
questions.trick: Denaturation kills 2$^\circ$/3$^\circ$ structure and activity; sequence (1$^\circ$) survives.

questions.q: Deficiency of vitamin B$_{12}$ causes
questions.explanation: Vitamin B$_{12}$ (cobalamin) is needed for red blood cell formation; its deficiency causes pernicious anaemia.
questions.trick: B$_{12}$ deficiency = pernicious anaemia, memorise the pairing.

questions.q: Vitamins that must be supplied regularly in the diet because they cannot be stored in the body are
questions.explanation: Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex, C) are excreted in urine and not stored appreciably, so regular dietary intake is required, unlike fat-soluble vitamins which are stored in adipose tissue and liver.
questions.trick: Water-soluble vitamins (B, C) aren't stored $\to$ need daily diet supply.

questions.q: The base found in DNA but not in RNA is
questions.explanation: DNA contains thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA instead; adenine, guanine and cytosine occur in both.
questions.trick: DNA has thymine, RNA has uracil instead — that's the swap to remember.

questions.q: The sugar component of RNA is
questions.explanation: RNA contains ribose (with an OH at the 2' position), whereas DNA contains 2-deoxyribose (lacking that oxygen).
questions.trick: RNA sugar = ribose; DNA sugar = 2-deoxyribose (one less O).

questions.q: In the DNA double helix, adenine pairs with thymine through
options: no hydrogen bonds, only van der Waals forces
questions.explanation: A=T pairing involves two hydrogen bonds, while G≡C pairing involves three, making G-C rich regions of DNA more thermally stable.
questions.trick: A=T two H-bonds; G$\equiv$C three H-bonds — GC-rich DNA is more stable.

questions.q: Cellulose differs from starch mainly in that cellulose has
options: β-1,4 glycosidic linkages, making it indigestible by humans
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a linear polymer of glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds; human digestive enzymes can hydrolyse only α-linkages (as in starch), so cellulose passes through undigested (roughage).
questions.trick: $\beta$-1,4 links in cellulose can't be cleaved by human (only $\alpha$-) enzymes.

questions.q: A nucleoside consists of
options: a nitrogenous base + a pentose sugar
questions.explanation: A nucleoside is base + sugar (no phosphate); adding a phosphate group gives a nucleotide, the repeating unit of nucleic acid polymers.
questions.trick: Nucleoside = base + sugar; add phosphate to get a nucleotide.

questions.q: Enzymes act as biological catalysts and are characterised by
options: catalysing reactions without being affected by pH
high substrate specificity and optimum activity in a narrow pH/temperature range
low specificity and activity over a wide pH/temperature range
questions.explanation: Enzymes (globular proteins) work on the lock-and-key/induced-fit principle giving high specificity, and their activity falls sharply outside an optimum pH and temperature range because the active protein conformation is disturbed.
questions.trick: Lock-and-key: enzymes are highly specific, active only in narrow pH/temp range.

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes an increase in blood clotting time?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is essential for the synthesis of clotting factors (prothrombin); its deficiency increases blood clotting time and causes excessive bleeding.
questions.trick: Vitamin K deficiency $\to$ increased blood clotting time (needed for prothrombin).

questions.q: Glycogen is often called 'animal starch' because it is
options: the highly branched storage polysaccharide of glucose in animals, analogous to starch in plants
questions.explanation: Glycogen, like amylopectin, is a branched glucose polymer, but even more highly branched; it serves as the glucose storage molecule in liver and muscle, the animal equivalent of starch.
questions.trick: Glycogen = highly branched glucose storage in animals, the 'animal starch'.

questions.q: An essential amino acid is one that
options: is synthesised in adequate amounts by the human body
must be supplied through the diet because the body cannot synthesise it in sufficient quantity
questions.explanation: Essential amino acids (e.g. valine, leucine, lysine) cannot be synthesised by the body in adequate amounts and must come from food; non-essential ones (e.g. glycine, alanine) can be synthesised in vivo.
questions.trick: Essential amino acid = body can't make enough, must come from diet.

questions.q: The peptide bond linking two amino acids is formed by
options: an addition reaction between two –COOH groups
a substitution reaction between two –NH$_2$ groups
a condensation reaction between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH$_2$ of another, releasing water
questions.explanation: The peptide (amide) bond forms when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of the next, eliminating a molecule of water.
questions.trick: Peptide bond: -COOH + -NH$_2$ condense, releasing H$_2$O, forming -CO-NH-.

questions.q: Which statement about DNA and RNA structure is correct?
options: DNA is usually single-stranded; RNA is double-stranded
DNA is usually double-stranded (helix); RNA is usually single-stranded
questions.explanation: DNA exists as a double helix of two complementary strands, whereas RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) is typically a single strand that may fold on itself.
questions.trick: DNA = double helix; RNA = usually single-stranded — fixed rule.

questions.q: The quaternary structure of a protein refers to
options: the spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits assembled together
the folding of a single polypeptide chain into a 3-D shape
the type of peptide bond present
the sequence of amino acids in a single chain
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure describes how multiple folded polypeptide subunits associate to form the functional protein, e.g. haemoglobin's four subunits; a single-chain protein has no quaternary structure.
questions.trick: Quaternary structure = multiple polypeptide subunits assembled together.

questions.q: Deficiency of vitamin D in children leads to
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency impairs calcium and phosphorus absorption/deposition in bones, causing rickets in children (osteomalacia in adults).
questions.trick: Vitamin D deficiency in children $\to$ rickets (bone mineralisation fails).

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly classifies monosaccharides, oligosaccharides, and polysaccharides?
options: Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further; oligosaccharides give 2-10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis; polysaccharides give a very large number of monosaccharide units
Monosaccharides always give 2 units on hydrolysis
Oligosaccharides always contain more than 100 units
questions.explanation: Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and cannot be broken down further by hydrolysis; oligosaccharides yield a small number (2-10) of monosaccharide units on hydrolysis, while polysaccharides (like starch, cellulose) yield very many units.
questions.trick: Hydrolysis units: mono = 1 (none), oligo = 2-10, poly = very many.

questions.q: Which functional group is common to both glucose and fructose, and which distinguishes them structurally?
options: Glucose has no OH groups; fructose has five
Both are aldoses; they differ only in ring size
Glucose is an aldohexose (has –CHO); fructose is a ketohexose (has C=O at C2); both have the molecular formula C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$
questions.explanation: Glucose and fructose are structural (functional) isomers with the same molecular formula, C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$, but glucose has an aldehyde group (aldohexose) while fructose has a ketone group at C-2 (ketohexose).
questions.trick: Glucose = aldohexose (-CHO); fructose = ketohexose (C=O at C2); same formula.

questions.q: Which evidence supports the presence of five –OH groups in the open-chain structure of glucose?
options: Glucose forms a pentaacetate on reaction with excess acetic anhydride
questions.explanation: When glucose reacts with excess acetic anhydride, all five hydroxyl groups get acetylated, forming glucose pentaacetate, which is direct evidence for five –OH groups in the open-chain structure.
questions.trick: Pentaacetate formation with excess Ac$_2$O proves glucose has five -OH groups.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about starch is INCORRECT?
options: Starch is a polymer of only fructose units
Starch gives a blue-black colour with iodine (mainly due to amylose)
Amylopectin is the branched component with $\alpha$-1,4 and $\alpha$-1,6 linkages
Amylose is the water-soluble, linear component with only $\alpha$-1,4 glycosidic linkages
questions.explanation: Starch is a polymer of $\alpha$-D-glucose units (not fructose), made of amylose and amylopectin components; the blue-black colour with iodine arises from iodine trapped inside the helical amylose coil.
questions.trick: Starch is a glucose polymer, NOT fructose — watch for that swapped trap.

questions.q: Which linkage type makes cellulose resistant to digestion by human digestive enzymes?
options: $\beta$-1,4 glycosidic linkage (human enzymes can only cleave $\alpha$-linkages)
questions.explanation: Human digestive enzymes (amylases) can hydrolyse only $\alpha$-glycosidic linkages (as in starch); cellulose's $\beta$-1,4 linkages cannot be cleaved by these enzymes, so cellulose acts as roughage rather than a nutrient in humans.
questions.trick: Human enzymes cleave only $\alpha$-links; cellulose's $\beta$-1,4 resists digestion.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the isoelectric point of an amino acid?
options: The pH at which the amino acid is fully positively charged
The pH at which the amino acid is fully negatively charged
The pH at which the amino acid exists predominantly as the zwitterion with no net charge, and hence shows minimum solubility and does not migrate in an electric field
The temperature at which the amino acid decomposes
questions.explanation: At the isoelectric point, the amino acid exists as a neutral dipolar zwitterion (equal positive and negative charge), has minimum solubility, and does not move towards either electrode in an electric field (used in electrophoretic separation).
questions.trick: Isoelectric point: zwitterion, net charge zero, minimum solubility, no migration.

questions.q: Which level of protein structure describes the actual three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide chain, stabilised by interactions such as hydrogen bonds, disulphide bridges, and hydrophobic interactions among side chains?
questions.explanation: Tertiary structure refers to the overall 3-D folding of a single polypeptide chain, held together by various non-covalent interactions and disulphide bonds between distant amino acid side chains, giving the protein its unique functional shape.
questions.trick: Tertiary structure = single chain's full 3-D fold (H-bonds, S-S, hydrophobic).

questions.q: Which of these statements about enzyme specificity is correct?
options: Enzymes catalyse a wide range of unrelated reactions with equal efficiency
Enzymes work equally well at all temperatures and pH values
Enzymes generally catalyse one specific reaction or a closely related set of reactions, based on the complementary shape of their active site to the substrate (lock-and-key or induced-fit model)
questions.explanation: Enzymes are highly specific because their active site has a particular 3-D shape and chemical environment that matches (or adapts to, in induced fit) only certain substrates; extreme pH or temperature denatures the enzyme and destroys this specificity.
questions.trick: Enzyme specificity = active site shape matches substrate (lock-key/induced fit).

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency is associated with beri-beri, characterised by nerve and cardiovascular problems?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B$_1$ (thiamine) deficiency leads to beri-beri, which affects the nervous and cardiovascular systems.
questions.trick: B$_1$ (thiamine) deficiency = beri-beri, nerve/cardiovascular symptoms.

questions.q: Which pair of vitamins are correctly classified as fat-soluble, capable of being stored in the body's adipose tissue?
questions.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and can be stored in the liver and adipose tissue, unlike water-soluble vitamins (B-complex, C), which must be regularly supplied in the diet since excess is excreted.
questions.trick: Fat-soluble, stored vitamins: A, D, E, K — remember 'ADEK'.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes a phosphodiester linkage found in DNA/RNA?
options: A hydrogen bond between complementary bases
A peptide bond between two amino acids
A glycosidic bond between two sugar units only
A bond linking the 3'-OH of one sugar to the 5'-phosphate of the next sugar in the nucleic acid backbone
questions.explanation: Successive nucleotides in a nucleic acid strand are joined by a phosphodiester linkage, in which a phosphate group bridges the 3'-OH of one sugar and the 5'-OH (as phosphate) of the next, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone.
questions.trick: Phosphodiester bond links 3'-OH of one sugar to 5'-phosphate of the next.

questions.q: Which base pairs with guanine in DNA, and how many hydrogen bonds are involved?
questions.explanation: In DNA, guanine pairs specifically with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds (G≡C), while adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds (A=T).
questions.trick: G pairs with C via 3 H-bonds; A pairs with T via 2 H-bonds.

questions.q: Which functional role does m-RNA play in protein synthesis?
options: It supplies energy for peptide bond formation
It stores the genetic code permanently in the nucleus
It carries the genetic code copied from DNA to the ribosome to direct amino acid sequence during protein synthesis
It forms the double helix with DNA
questions.explanation: Messenger RNA (m-RNA) is synthesised as a complementary copy of a DNA gene (transcription) and carries this genetic information to ribosomes, where it directs the sequence of amino acids added during translation (protein synthesis).
questions.trick: mRNA copies DNA's code and carries it to ribosomes for translation.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why glucose does NOT give certain typical aldehyde reactions (like Schiff's test) despite having an aldehyde group in its open-chain structure?
options: Glucose exists predominantly in a cyclic hemiacetal form in solution, in which the free aldehyde group is masked
Glucose is not soluble in water
Glucose has no aldehyde group at all
questions.explanation: In aqueous solution, glucose exists mainly as a six-membered cyclic hemiacetal (pyranose form), where the aldehyde carbon (C1) is bonded to an oxygen from the C5-OH group, masking the free aldehyde and explaining the negative Schiff's test.
questions.trick: Glucose's cyclic hemiacetal form masks the aldehyde $\to$ negative Schiff's test.

questions.q: Which structural feature explains why sucrose is a non-reducing sugar while maltose is a reducing sugar?
options: In sucrose, the glycosidic bond forms between the anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose, leaving no free anomeric carbon to reduce Fehling's/Tollens' reagent; in maltose one anomeric carbon remains free
Sucrose has no glycosidic bond at all
Sucrose is a polysaccharide while maltose is a monosaccharide
questions.explanation: In sucrose, the glycosidic linkage involves the anomeric carbons of BOTH glucose (C1) and fructose (C2), leaving no free reducing group; in maltose the glycosidic bond involves only one anomeric carbon, leaving the other free to reduce Fehling's/Tollens' reagent.
questions.trick: Sucrose locks both anomeric carbons; maltose leaves one free to reduce.

questions.q: Which of the following amino acids would be classified as non-essential?
options: Glycine (the body can synthesise it in adequate amounts)
questions.explanation: Glycine is a non-essential amino acid because the human body can synthesise it in sufficient quantities; valine, leucine and lysine are essential amino acids that must be obtained from the diet.
questions.trick: Body synthesises glycine adequately $\to$ it's non-essential, unlike valine/leucine/lysine.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares nucleosides and nucleotides?
options: A nucleoside is base + sugar + phosphate; a nucleotide is base + sugar only
A nucleoside and a nucleotide are identical in composition
A nucleoside is base + sugar; a nucleotide additionally has a phosphate group esterified to the sugar
questions.explanation: A nucleoside consists of a nitrogenous base linked to a pentose sugar; when a phosphate group is attached to the sugar (typically at the 5' position), the resulting unit is called a nucleotide, the monomer of nucleic acids.
questions.trick: Nucleoside = base+sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate ester.

questions.q: Excess intake of which vitamin can be toxic because it is fat-soluble and accumulates in the body rather than being excreted?
options: Vitamin A (hypervitaminosis A can cause toxicity)
questions.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins like A, D, E and K accumulate in fatty tissue and the liver since they are not readily excreted; excess intake, particularly of Vitamin A, can lead to toxicity (hypervitaminosis), unlike water-soluble vitamins which are excreted in excess.
questions.trick: Fat-soluble vitamins (like A) accumulate, not excreted $\to$ toxicity risk.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about the primary structure of a protein and denaturation?
options: Denaturation disrupts secondary/tertiary structure and biological activity, but the primary structure (amino acid sequence held by peptide bonds) is generally unaffected
The primary structure refers to the 3-D shape of the protein
Denaturation always breaks the peptide bonds that define the primary structure
Denaturation has no effect on protein structure or function
questions.explanation: Denaturing agents (heat, extreme pH, heavy metal ions) disrupt the weaker non-covalent interactions (H-bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that maintain secondary and tertiary structure, destroying biological activity, while the covalent peptide bonds of the primary sequence remain intact.
questions.trick: Denaturation spares covalent peptide bonds (primary structure); wrecks 2$^\circ$/3$^\circ$ only.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly lists a key structural difference between DNA and RNA regarding their sugar component?
options: Both contain identical sugars with no difference
DNA contains 2-deoxyribose (lacking an OH at C2'); RNA contains ribose (with an OH at C2')
Neither DNA nor RNA contains a sugar component
questions.explanation: DNA's sugar, 2-deoxyribose, lacks the hydroxyl group at the 2' carbon present in RNA's sugar, ribose; this structural difference contributes to DNA's greater chemical stability, suited to long-term genetic storage.
questions.trick: DNA sugar lacks 2'-OH (deoxyribose); RNA sugar keeps it (ribose).
